extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics and elementary number theory (readers studying proofs and basic algebra/number theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook material and exercises on relations, gcd/lcm, unique prime factorisation, functions (definitions, images/preimages), and basic proof techniques (induction, Bézout, Euclid's lemma).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique reduced fraction representing a rational number
rubrics_metrics.description: If a/b = c/d = r then there is a unique smallest fraction x/y = r so that a = kx, c = nx, b = ky, d = ny for some integers k,n. That is, the fractions a/b and c/d reduce to the same fraction x/y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea given: choose n maximal so that a > n x, deduce a - n x = x and hence a is a multiple of x and similarly for b. Note remark that this property can fail in other rings (hint to unique factorisation domains and non-examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid's lemma (primal divisibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is prime and p | ab then p | a or p | b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma is a key tool used to prove uniqueness of prime factorisation and is applied in examples such as: from ab = pc deduce a/p = c/b and then arguing with reduced fractions to show p divides a when p ∤ b.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Bézout's lemma to compare multiples/divisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Bézout's lemma: for gcd d = gcd(a,b) there exist x,y ∈ Z with d = ax + by; use this to relate dL and dM and deduce divisibility relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example application in proving gcd(a,b)·lcm(a,b)=|ab|: let L = |ab|/d; to show L divides any common multiple M of a and b, multiply equality d = ax+by by M and rearrange to show dL | dM and hence L | M.

rubrics_metrics.name: gcd(a,b)·lcm(a,b) = |a·b| (Lemma 9.5.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let d = gcd(a,b) and L = |ab|/d. Then L is a common multiple of a and b and any other common multiple M satisfies |L| ≤ |M|, so L is the least common multiple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: write a = dk, b = dn to show L = |an| = |bk| so a|L and b|L. For minimality, for any common multiple M write M = ap = bq and use Bézout's identity to show dL divides dM, hence L|M. The lemma relies on the divisibility facts and Bézout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic (existence and uniqueness of prime factorisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every integer n > 1 can be written as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique up to permutation of the primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence proved by strong induction: if n composite write n = a b with 1<a,b<n and apply inductive hypothesis to a,b. Uniqueness proved by assuming two prime decompositions, cancel common primes, then use Euclid's lemma to show the smallest remaining prime divides a factor on the other side and thus must appear on both sides, contradiction if they were disjoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a function (as a special relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : A → B is a non-empty subset of A×B with two properties: (1) for every a∈A there exists b∈B with (a,b)∈f; (2) if (a,b)∈f and (a,c)∈f then b=c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: totality (every input has an output) and single-valuedness (well-defined). Alternate phrasing: for every a∈A there is some b with f(a)=b, and if f(a)=b and f(a)=c then b=c. Vertical line test is the geometric analogue for R→R functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-definedness (single-valuedness) anti-pattern and test
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-definedness: if f(a)=b1 and f(a)=b2 then b1=b2. The converse (a=b implies f(a)=f(b)) is not the definition of injectivity; confusing the implication directions is a common mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the contrapositive or equality-based tests carefully. The text warns: a common mistake is giving the converse implication instead of the required implication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain, codomain and range distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Given f : A → B, A is the domain, B is the codomain, and the range is rng f = {b ∈ B | ∃a ∈ A s.t. f(a)=b}. The range need not equal the codomain (example f(x)=x^2 has codomain R but range [0,∞)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Range is always a subset of codomain. The distinction is useful because often the codomain is easy to write while the range may be harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image and preimage of sets (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : A → B and C⊆A, D⊆B: image f(C) = {f(x): x∈C}. Preimage f^{-1}(D) = {x∈A: f(x)∈D}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: preimage of a singleton {y} may be empty, one element, multiple elements, or infinite. Notational warning: f^{-1} denotes preimage in general and is not necessarily the inverse function; context matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of images and preimages with set operations (Theorem 10.3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key identities: (i) C ⊆ f^{-1}(f(C)) and f(f^{-1}(D)) ⊆ D; (iii) f(C1 ∩ C2) ⊆ f(C1) ∩ f(C2) (not necessarily equality); (iv) f(C1 ∪ C2) = f(C1) ∪ f(C2); (vi) f^{-1}(D1 ∩ D2) = f^{-1}(D1) ∩ f^{-1}(D2) and f^{-1}(D1 ∪ D2) = f^{-1}(D1) ∪ f^{-1}(D2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preimages commute with unions and intersections (equalities). Images commute with unions (equality) but only satisfy a subset relation for intersections in general. Proofs provided for sample items; counterexamples may show converses fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof technique: how to prove set inclusion/equality for images/preimages
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove A ⊆ B for image/preimage statements, take an arbitrary element in the left set and show it belongs to the right set via definitions of image/preimage and element-wise reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text demonstrates typical element-chasing proofs (e.g., to prove f(C1 ∩ C2) ⊆ f(C1) ∩ f(C2) pick b∈f(C1∩C2), get a∈C1∩C2 with f(a)=b, deduce b∈f(C1) and b∈f(C2)). These are standard techniques for these identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invertibility criterion for functions (existence of inverse)
rubrics_metrics.description: A function is 'undoable' (invertible) when for every y in the codomain the preimage of {y} contains exactly one element of the domain; equivalently each y has a unique x with f(x)=y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In finite settings this forces domain and codomain to have the same size. Practically, invertibility requires both injectivity (unique preimage) and surjectivity (every codomain element has a preimage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and equivalent formulations of injectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: f is injective (one-to-one) if for all a1≠a2 we have f(a1)≠f(a2), equivalently if f(a1)=f(a2) then a1=a2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: use the equality-based formulation for proofs (assume f(a1)=f(a2) and deduce a1=a2). Common pitfall: confusing the implication direction; 'a1=a2 ⇒ f(a1)=f(a2)' just restates well-definedness and is the wrong property for injectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove a function is injective (pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard proof pattern: assume f(a1)=f(a2) and manipulate algebraically/structurally to deduce a1=a2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked example: f(x)=7x-3 — assume 7a1-3 = 7a2-3, cancel constants to get a1=a2. This pattern is recommended because equality manipulations are familiar.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove a function is not injective (counterexample pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show non-injectivity, exhibit distinct a1≠a2 in the domain with f(a1)=f(a2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worked example: f(x)=x^2 on R is not injective since f(-1)=f(1)=1. Presenting an explicit pair suffices to disprove injectivity.
